summary: Describes how mail clients and servers using IMAP, POP3 and ACAP can upgrade a plain connection to an encrypted one with TLS. It also defines a PLAIN login method for protocols that lack a simple password command. Later RFCs have updated it.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains how IMAP, POP3 and ACAP can switch an open connection to TLS encryption. It also sets rules for checking the server and protecting passwords.

subtitle: How IMAP, POP3 and ACAP begin TLS on an existing connection, and how clients check the server.

tldr.problem: IMAP, POP3 and ACAP can send passwords over an unencrypted connection. Attackers on the network may listen to or alter that traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The protocols add STARTTLS or STLS commands that begin TLS on the existing connection. The RFC also sets rules for cipher suites, server identity checks, clear-text logins and the PLAIN SASL mechanism.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 4616, RFC 7817 and RFC 8314. Read those updates with this specification.

sections.title: Why Mail Protocols Use TLS
sections.content:
Transport Layer Security (TLS), formerly called SSL, protects an application connection from eavesdropping and tampering. The RFC applies it to IMAP, POP3 and ACAP because attackers can listen to or hijack these connections.

TLS works alongside authentication methods. It lets sites protect network traffic without replacing their existing password databases. The RFC also defines the PLAIN SASL mechanism for protocols that lack a simple password command.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS encrypts the connection between a mail client and server. This protects passwords and other data while they cross the network.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
Implementations must support the cipher suite TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA so compliant clients and servers can be configured to work together. Other cipher suites are optional. Clients and servers should offer a mode that refuses authentication until encryption is active.

Implementations must be configurable to reject clear-text login unless an encryption layer of adequate strength is active. Both sides must check whether TLS achieved acceptable privacy or authentication. The RFC leaves that policy decision to each implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must check that TLS succeeded and meets their security policy. A client or server must be configurable to reject clear-text passwords when encryption is not active.

sections.title: Checking the Server Identity
sections.content:
During TLS negotiation, the client must compare the hostname it used to open the connection with the identity in the server's certificate. It must use that original hostname, not a name obtained from an insecure remote source. Matching ignores letter case, and a certificate may use a wildcard as its left-most name component.

If a certificate has a dNSName subject alternative name, the client should use it. A match with any certificate name is acceptable. If no name matches, the client should ask the user to confirm or end the connection and report that the server identity is suspect.
sections.plainLanguage: Before trusting the connection, the client checks that the server certificate names the host it contacted. If the names do not match, the client should ask the user or stop.

sections.title: Starting TLS in Each Protocol
sections.content:
IMAP and ACAP use the STARTTLS command; POP3 uses STLS. Servers advertise support through their capability information. IMAP and ACAP accept STARTTLS only before authentication, and POP3 accepts STLS only in its AUTHORIZATION state.

After the server agrees, TLS negotiation begins on the current connection. The client must wait for that negotiation to finish before sending another command. It must discard capability information learned before TLS and should ask for capabilities again, because an attacker could have changed the earlier list. ACAP servers send a fresh greeting after TLS starts.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks to start TLS on the connection it already has. After TLS starts, the client asks for the server's capabilities again because the earlier list may have been changed.

sections.title: Clear-Text Login and PLAIN
sections.content:
An IMAP server may advertise LOGINDISABLED to show that the clear-text LOGIN command is unavailable. A server that supports STARTTLS must support this capability on unencrypted connections. A compliant client must not send LOGIN when it sees the capability, though an attacker could remove it before TLS starts.

The PLAIN SASL mechanism sends an authorization identity, a NUL character, an authentication identity, another NUL character and a clear-text password in one client message. Each field must support up to 255 octets, and text uses UTF-8. PLAIN must not be advertised or used unless strong encryption is active, except where backward compatibility requires it.
sections.plainLanguage: PLAIN sends the password without encryption, so it must be used only after a strong encryption layer starts. On an unencrypted IMAP connection, LOGINDISABLED tells a compliant client not to send LOGIN.

sections.title: Limits and Risks of TLS
sections.content:
TLS protects data only while it crosses the network. Server administrators can still access messages, and later transfers may expose them. The RFC says TLS does not replace end-to-end message security.

A person in the middle can remove a STARTTLS capability, fake a failure or push the connection toward a weaker mechanism. Clients should warn when privacy is inactive or refuse connections without acceptable security. PLAIN also gives the server the user's password, which may let that server impersonate the user to other services that use the same password.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS protects a connection, but it does not hide messages from the server that receives them. Clients should detect failed or weak protection, and PLAIN exposes the password to the server.
